lessons.title: The lactation cycle and herd reproduction
lessons.html:
A cow must calve to milk

A dairy cow produces milk after calving. Milk yield rises to a peak in the first weeks to couple of months of lactation, then gradually declines. The cow is dried off before her next calving to let the udder regenerate. Herd profitability depends on getting cows back in calf on time so that each cow spends most of her life in productive lactation.

The cycle

  1. Calving and early lactation: yield rises fast, but appetite lags behind, so cows lose body condition. This is the highest-risk period for metabolic disease.
  2. Peak and mid-lactation: cows should be inseminated and confirmed pregnant in this period.
  3. Late lactation: yield declines; cows regain body condition.
  4. Dry period: milking stops before calving, as set by the farm's protocol with the vet. Dry cows need their own feeding and management, especially in the weeks just before calving (the transition period).

Reproduction management

  • Heat detection: watch for standing heat, mounting, restlessness, mucus discharge and drop in milk. Use tail paint, activity meters or heat detectors, and observe at set times each day. Missed heats cost money.
  • Insemination: artificial insemination (AI) by trained inseminators allows use of proven bulls; some farms use bulls for cows that do not conceive to AI.
  • Pregnancy diagnosis: by the vet, by rectal palpation or ultrasound, at regular herd visits.
  • Records: calving dates, heats, inseminations, sires used, pregnancy results.

Key reproductive measures

MeasureMeaning
Calving intervalDays between successive calvings
Days openDays from calving to conception
Heat detection rateProportion of eligible heats detected
Conception rateProportion of inseminations resulting in pregnancy

Set targets with your manager and vet and review them monthly.

lessons.title: Milk yield, quality and herd improvement
lessons.html:
What drives milk yield

  • Genetics: breed and the genetic merit of sires and dams.
  • Nutrition: energy, protein, fibre, minerals and water intake.
  • Health: mastitis, lameness and metabolic disease all cut yield.
  • Comfort: shade, clean dry lying areas, good walkways and calm handling.
  • Stage of lactation and age: yield peaks in early lactation and in mature cows.
  • Milking management: consistent routines and intervals.

Heat stress

High-yielding cows produce a lot of metabolic heat. In hot, humid weather they eat less, produce less and show poorer fertility. Provide shade, plenty of cool water near the parlour and in camps, fans and sprinklers in holding yards, and feed in the cooler parts of the day.

Milk components and quality

Payment usually depends on volume, butterfat and protein, with quality criteria such as somatic cell count (SCC, an indicator of udder infection) and bacterial count (an indicator of milking hygiene and cooling). Low butterfat can indicate rations short of effective fibre.

Milk recording

Regular milk recording measures each cow's yield and components, and often SCC. Use it to:

  • Identify high and low producers.
  • Pick out cows with high SCC for mastitis checks.
  • Adjust group feeding.
  • Make culling and breeding decisions.

Body condition scoring

Score cows regularly on the scale your farm uses. Cows that lose too much condition after calving have more fertility problems; cows that are too fat at calving have more calving difficulties and metabolic diseases.

Herd improvement and culling

Choose AI sires for traits that matter for your system: yield and components, fertility, udder health, longevity and, for pasture systems, moderate size. Cull cows for persistent mastitis, chronic lameness, repeated failure to conceive and low production, so that replacements raised from the best cows lift the herd.

Key points

  • Cows must calve regularly to keep producing milk.
  • Good heat detection and timely insemination drive the calving interval.
  • Yield depends on genetics, nutrition, health, comfort and milking routine.
  • Manage heat stress with shade, water and cooling.
  • Use milk recording and condition scoring for decisions.
